item.title: Teachers likely paid
item.description: THE Fijian Teachers Association is assuming teachers at the center of unpaid salary reports have now been paid, despite receiving no confirmation from those affected. FTA’s general secretary Paula Manumanunitoga said the association had received no official complaint from teachers still waiting for their salaries.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fijian Teachers Association is assuming teachers at the center of unpaid salary reports have now been paid, despite receiving no confirmation from those affected.

FTA’s general secretary Paula Manumanunitoga said the association had received no official complaint from teachers still waiting for their salaries.

“I have not gotten any confirmation from any of those affected. But they are quiet. I believe they have received their pay,” he said.

Mr Manumanunitoga said no teacher had returned to the association to report that they remained unpaid.

“No official complaints have been filed yet about the unpaid salaries.”

As of Monday, 118 of the 134 affected teachers had been confirmed to have received their pay.

item.content:encoded:
SUVA’S St Joseph’s Secondary School is proudly celebrating 70 years of education, faith, service and achievement this month.

The milestone marks seven decades of shaping young women and preparing them to contribute positively to their families, communities and Fiji.

Founded through the dedication of the Sisters of St Joseph of Cluny, the school has built a strong tradition of academic excellence, discipline and compassion.

item.title: 43,000 students assessed
item.description: ALMOST 43,000 Pacific students sat the 2025 Pacific Islands Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (PILNA), with results highlighting the importance of data in improving classroom learning across the region. The assessment was administered across 1098 schools in 15 member countries, reaching almost 23,000 Year 4 students and more than 20,000 Year 6 students.
item.content:encoded:
ALMOST 43,000 Pacific students sat the 2025 Pacific Islands Literacy and Numeracy Assessment (PILNA), with results highlighting the importance of data in improving classroom learning across the region.

The assessment was administered across 1098 schools in 15 member countries, reaching almost 23,000 Year 4 students and more than 20,000 Year 6 students.

Australian High Commission’s counsellor for human development Emmeline Carrick said the PILNA report provided critical evidence to support education reform across the Pacific.

Speaking at the launch of the 2025 PILNA report in Suva yesterday, Ms Carrick said the findings would help governments and education stakeholders better understand the challenges facing students and strengthen literacy and numeracy outcomes.

“This report provides valuable data that ministries of education across the Pacific can use to inform practical policy decisions, curriculum reform, resource allocation and strategic planning,” she said.

“This is not to provide any sort of ranking, but to support reflection, accountability and continuous improvement, and enable targeted interventions to support learners who are falling behind.”

item.title: Push for tiered cane payments
item.description: CANE top-up payments from Government should be channelled through a tiered system to ensure active growers are properly compensated, according to concerns raised during parliamentary scrutiny. During the Ministry of Sugar Industry 2021–2022 Annual Report presentation, Parliamentary Standing Committee on Economic Affairs chairperson Sakiusa Tubuna said there were concerns that subsidies were being
item.content:encoded:
CANE top-up payments from Government should be channelled through a tiered system to ensure active growers are properly compensated, according to concerns raised during parliamentary scrutiny.

During the Ministry of Sugar Industry 2021–2022 Annual Report presentation, Parliamentary Standing Committee on Economic Affairs chairperson Sakiusa Tubuna said there were concerns that subsidies were being distributed to all growers, despite uneven production performance.

“There is considerable subsidy provided to the farmers,” he said.

“One of our concerns is that the subsidy is provided to all of the farmers without any clear targeting, and even if 20 per cent of the farmers are providing 80 per cent of the total tonnage.

“The other 80 per cent are farmers that are not performing.”

He said a new approach was needed to better reward highly productive growers.

In response, Ministry of Sugar Industry’s director operations Praneel Naidu agreed it was one of the unfortunate issues the ministry was dealing with.

“Unfortunately, our grant is set as such that around 50 per cent or more goes to the cane top-up payment,” he said.

“So generally, everyone has access to that, but if you want a way forward, then we need to set a tier system.”

He said, however, a tiered approach may work in some programs and not in others.

“We are also looking at setting up a system that is more reward-based rather than a generic payout to all farmers no matter what they achieve,” he said.

“We had introduced it in the farmer incentive program, but it has not really yielded the results that we required for it, so this year we are going to re-divert it to the green cane farmers development program.

“There are some areas that we are manoeuvring, but it is a work in progress at the moment.”

item.title: Call for inquiry into police
item.description: THE Fiji Council of Social Services (FCOSS) has renewed its call for a commission of inquiry into the Fiji Police Force, warning that weak independent oversight could undermine Fiji’s democracy. FCOSS program’s manager Josaia Tokoni made the submission yesterday to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights during its consideration of the Fiji Police Bill 2026.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Council of Social Services (FCOSS) has renewed its call for a commission of inquiry into the Fiji Police Force, warning that weak independent oversight could undermine Fiji’s democracy.

FCOSS program’s manager Josaia Tokoni made the submission yesterday to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Justice, Law and Human Rights during its consideration of the Fiji Police Bill 2026.

Mr Tokoni said FCOSS had called for a commission of inquiry three times – in 2021, 2023 and again in December last year – following concerns including the death of a person at a Beqa village linked to alleged police brutality.

“Our national precedence set it plainly at the time – when law enforcement bypasses the court and takes human life into its own hands, the foundation of our democracy begins to crumble,” he said.

FCOSS welcomed provisions requiring the use of force by police to be proportionate and a last resort, greater civil society involvement in police training, community policing and quarterly reporting of complaints and disciplinary action.

However, Mr Tokoni said stronger independent oversight was needed.

“We are not here to oppose any reform,” he added.

“However, we are here because in our experience, the gap between good intention and good outcome in this country usually comes down to one question: who is watching when something goes wrong?”

FCOSS recommended mandatory independent review of complaints involving human rights violations or excessive force that are summarily dismissed.

Mr Tokoni also raised concerns about covert surveillance, tracking and biometric powers.

“Given Fiji’s history of coups and political interference, powers this broad concentrated in one institution, create the risk of misuse against civil society, political opponents or journalists.”

item.title: More time for A-G’s Office to serve court papers
item.description: THE High Court has given the Attorney-General’s Office more time to personally serve contempt of court proceedings on Feroz Gulam Mohammed, who is overseas. item.content:encoded:
THE High Court has given the Attorney-General’s Office more time to personally serve contempt of court proceedings on Feroz Gulam Mohammed, who is overseas.

The matter was called before Justices Siainiu Fa’alogo Bull, Dane Tuiqereqere and Savenaca Banuve recently, when deputy State solicitor Ofa Solimailagi told the court that efforts had been made to establish Mr Mohammed’s address in New Zealand and Canada.

The Attorney-General initiated contempt of court proceedings against Mr Mohammed over alleged scandalous comments he made about Chief Justice Salesi Temo in a video posted on Facebook. The High Court is sitting as a three-member panel to hear the contempt of court charge.

Ms Solimailagi told the court that she had been told Mr Mohammed has an address in Auckland but is currently in Canada attending a family wedding.

She presented three options to the court — personal service, substituted service or wait for Mr Mohammed’s return to Fiji. The court indicated it was inclined to give more time for Mr Mohammed to return to Fiji and allow an opportunity for his legal representation to be properly established.

The matter is adjourned to September 21 for hearing.

item.title: Lateef admits to possessing drugs
item.description: FORMER Suva lawyer Shazran Abdul Lateef has admitted to possessing methamphetamine and marijuana, as well as breaching his bail conditions in 2019. The 65-year-old entered a guilty plea before Magistrate Lisiate Fotofili yesterday to possessing 1.8 grams of methamphetamine and 4.0 grams of marijuana on December 10, 2019. He also pleaded guilty to breaching his bail conditions.
item.content:encoded:
FORMER Suva lawyer Shazran Abdul Lateef has admitted to possessing methamphetamine and marijuana, as well as breaching his bail conditions in 2019.

The 65-year-old entered a guilty plea before Magistrate Lisiate Fotofili yesterday to possessing 1.8 grams of methamphetamine and 4.0 grams of marijuana on December 10, 2019. He also pleaded guilty to breaching his bail conditions.

Mr Lateef’s production order was extended, and the case has been adjourned to September 18 for mitigation submissions.

He is currently serving a 44-month prison sentence for a separate 2019 incident involving the unlawful possession of 9.5 grams of methamphetamine and 3.5 grams of marijuana at a hotel in Suva.

item.title: Thief’s appeal successful
item.description: AN appeal by a serial thief was allowed by the High Court in Suva which reduced his 22-month prison sentence after finding the lower court committed a double-counting error by picking an overly high starting point. Justice Sunil Sharma quashed the sentence imposed on Atelemo Waqa by the Nadi Magistrate’s Court and re-sentenced him to 16 months and 17 days’ imprisonment.
item.content:encoded:
AN appeal by a serial thief was allowed by the High Court in Suva which reduced his 22-month prison sentence after finding the lower court committed a double-counting error by picking an overly high starting point.

Justice Sunil Sharma quashed the sentence imposed on Atelemo Waqa by the Nadi Magistrate’s Court and re-sentenced him to 16 months and 17 days’ imprisonment.

Waqa had pleaded guilty to stealing a mobile valued at $350 from a Total Health Pharmacy employee in Nadi this year.

The court was told that Waqa went to the pharmacy claiming he wanted to buy haemorrhoid tablets. Once inside, he distracted the employee, took her phone from beneath the counter, and fled. CCTV footage later identified him.

The magistrate’s court initially sentenced Waqa to 22 months and 17 days imprisonment with a 16-month non-parole period.

On appeal, Justice Sharma held that the magistrate erred by adopting a two-year starting point at the higher end of the tariff and adding another year for aggravating factors.

The court noted that this was Waqa’s fourth conviction for theft-related offences within the past 10 years.

Justice Sharma set aside the non-parole period, leaving early release to the Corrections Commissioner’s discretion.
